title: Poland's $13bn naval build-out and Ukraine's silent drone export channel
subhead: NATO's eastern flank is buying submarines, the Saudi navy is localizing under a Saudi-US-Italian stack, and Kyiv's much-advertised drone export fast track has issued zero permits in its first three months. Procurement paperwork, not procurement announcements, is the story.

sections.heading: Ukraine's drone export fast track: three months, zero permits
sections.body:
Ukraine's Cabinet adopted a special export channel for arms on July 1, 2026 under Cabinet Resolution No. 875, published in the government gazette Uryadovyi Kurier on July 8 and effective that day. The pitch was a 30-day decision with no hearing before the Interagency Commission on Military-Technical Cooperation and Export Control, and a deemed-approval rule: if the Defense Ministry or the security services stayed silent past their deadline, the transfer counted as cleared.

Three months later, no permit had been issued under it, according to LB.ua reporting of October 2 cited by Defense-Aerospace. The lists that activate the procedure were not in place, and the government had received proposals to rewrite it. The head of the export-clearing commission said the procedure had not started working.

The one documented sale of finished Ukrainian strike drones to a NATO military went around the fast track entirely. On the same July 1 date, Ukraine's State Export Control Service cleared a batch of F10 FPV strike drones from manufacturer F-Drones for the U.S. military under the old procedure. The U.S. buyer, UDD Tech Corp (the U.S. arm of F-Drones), had entered the F10 in Gauntlet I of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program. The leaderboard as of October 1 ranks UDD sixth of 11 winners with 72.9 points, 2,000 drones ordered, all listed as shipped and accepted, plus a 1,320-unit bonus order not yet shipped.

The relationship then moved to U.S. soil. On June 29, Rep. Marcy Kaptur's office announced UDD had chosen the Village of Holland, Ohio, for its first U.S. assembly and manufacturing center, and the Ohio Tax Credit Authority approved a nine-year, 1.642% tax credit the same day. The authority's scope-of-work document describes a commitment to 300 full-time jobs and $18.4 million in new annual payroll by December 31, 2029, and a 12-year operating requirement at the site. F-Drones CEO Stas Khutor framed it as moving technology: 'The next step is to share the technology to produce these drones on American soil.'

The program's own rules explain why that matters. The DDP Supply Chain Framework, version 2 dated July 23, 2026, requires U.S. final assembly from Phase 3, which opened September 28. Phase 3 is a $450 million request for about 60,000 drones with payloads and safe-and-arm devices. UDD competed in Gauntlet II at Fort Carson in August but did not finish in the top five, so it was not among the ten vendors fast-tracked into Phase 3.
sections.whyItMatters: The legal route to buy finished Ukrainian drones exists on paper only. The one buyer on record is steering the supplier into U.S. production, which means Ukraine's drone industry may export capacity before it exports finished systems.

sections.heading: Poland's naval modernisation adds up to a $13bn market
sections.body:
Poland is rebuilding both its surface and undersea fleets, and Shephard Defence Insight puts the resulting procurement opportunity at roughly $13 billion through the 2030s, with further buys expected beyond that window.

The anchor deal on the undersea side is a June 29, 2026 contract with Saab for three A26 submarines. On the surface side, Warsaw is replacing Soviet-era hulls with a mix of domestic shipyards and foreign partners, and Shephard reports the programme is structured so that further opportunities keep coming into the next decade rather than being settled in one tranche.

Poland's naval spending sits inside a broader eastern-flank pattern: the countries closest to Russia are buying high-end platforms while simultaneously trying to keep industrial work at home. Shephard's coverage of the Polish programme treats the shipbuilding pipeline as a market forecast, not a one-off order.
sections.whyItMatters: Central Europe is no longer just buying used Western equipment. Poland is writing a decade-long naval acquisition plan, which turns it into one of the largest European naval customers outside the big four producers.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia's two naval projects and the localization stack behind them
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense detailed two naval programmes on November 1 that together do what most Gulf procurement announcements only gesture at: they put industrial localization in the contract terms.

The Sarawat Project covers eight Avante 2200 corvettes from Navantia across two phases. Phase one delivered five ships (HMS Al Jubail, HMS Al Diriyah, HMS Hail, HMS Jazan, HMS Unayzah) with simulators, sea-trial crew training and land-based test facilities. Phase two covers HMS Al Madinah, HMS NEOM and HMS AlUla, plus an integrated logistics package, specialized training for over 100 Saudi engineers, and localization of vessel assembly, systems integration and maintenance.

The parallel Tuwaiq Project covers four Multi-Mission Surface Combatants (HMS King Saud, HMS King Fahd, HMS King Abdullah, HMS King Salman), executed with Lockheed Martin and Fincantieri in coordination with GAMI, and includes expanding King Abdulaziz Naval Base in Jubail plus maintenance and simulation training centers. Naval News identified the first MMSC, HMS King Saud, on the new syncrolift at FMM on December 20, 2025.

The stated driver is coastline: the Royal Saudi Naval Forces are tasked with securing Red Sea and Arabian Gulf approaches and critical maritime corridors under the MoD Development Program approved in February 2018.
sections.whyItMatters: Riyadh is buying the same ships everyone buys but contracting for the assembly line and the engineers as well. That is the difference between a customer and a future producer.

sections.heading: Russia writes off the Pyotr Velikiy
sections.body:
The Russian Navy has cancelled modernization of the Kirov-class nuclear battlecruiser Pyotr Velikiy, first reported by TASS and covered by Naval News on November 1. A special commission reached a preliminary decision that the ship is 'not subject to restoration' because of its wear and tear, per Vladimir Maltsev, head of the All-Russian Movement of Support of the Fleet. The final decision has not been announced, and the ship remains in limbo between modernization and scrapping.

The proximate cause is money already spent elsewhere. Sister ship Admiral Nakhimov ran roughly eight years late in its own modernization, from 2018 to 2026, with the total refit taking about 12 years. Estimates for the Nakhimov refurbishment run as high as $5 billion, which appears to have consumed the funding earmarked for a matching upgrade of the Pyotr Velikiy. Pyotr Velikiy had been the sole active Kirov in service for roughly 25 years and has been at Severomorsk since late 2022.

The Nakhimov now fields Zircon hypersonic missiles and S-400 air-defense systems with up to 176 primary vertical launch cells; a full weapons loadout could cost around $500 million depending on the munition mix.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's surface fleet is contracting to one modernized capital ship bought at roughly $5 billion and twelve years. The Kuznetsov and now the Pyotr Velikiy show the same pattern: repair bills that exceed the value of the hulls.

sections.heading: NATO's industry strategy carries no legal force, and the contracts know it
sections.body:
NATO's July 7-8 Ankara summit produced two documents that trade coverage routinely merges. The Summit Declaration set a procurement floor of 'more than $50 billion' in new capability deals. A day later, allied leaders endorsed the Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation (SYNC), the Alliance's first rewrite of its industry-engagement framework since 2013.

Read in full, SYNC describes itself as voluntary, with 'no direct funding implications or legal impact' (Appendix 1, principle 2), and confines its measures to the pre-competitive phase of capability development. Its new instruments are the NATO Front Door for Industry (a procurement-portal aggregator), the NATO Engine (a capacity-matching network for manufacturers and non-traditional suppliers), and an unclassified version of the aggregated demand signal drawn from the NATO Defence Planning Process. The agency that actually negotiates and signs joint-procurement contracts, NSPA, has operated since 1958 and is untouched by the strategy.

The clearest case is Saab GlobalEye, headlined at the summit as a joint procurement by 11 Allies (Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Romania, Sweden) to replace part of the Boeing E-3 fleet. NATO's own text calls it a joint procurement, not a contract, and gives no aircraft count; a figure of up to ten aircraft appears in Secretary General Mark Rutte's forum remarks as reported by Breaking Defense, not in NATO's news release. Per Defense-Aerospace, Saab confirmed no signed contract and no firm order existed as of late August 2026, with agency-level negotiations with NSPA only beginning.

The financial figures are similarly elastic. The procurement floor appears on NATO pages as 'more than $50 billion' on one and 'more than €50 billion' on another, which sets floors of roughly €43bn and roughly $58bn respectively — a 15% gap that disappears because both round to about half a hundred billion. The summit also stated €70 billion for Ukraine in 2026, with no methodology published for either figure. The CNAD Implementation Plan meant to convert SYNC's three objectives into taskings was due by October 2026 and had not been published as of Defense-Aerospace's assessment.
sections.whyItMatters: The West's flagship industrial-coordination instrument is a voluntary engagement framework standing next to its own unrelated procurement channels. The benchmark to watch is GlobalEye: NATO's last AEW selection, the Boeing E-7A in 2023, was abandoned in 2025 without a single aircraft delivered.

sections.heading: Autonomy and the uncrewed edge: AUTOWARCOM's funding problem, GPS-free ground swarms, and Israel's crewed bet
sections.body:
Three data points on where unmanned programmes actually stand.

AUTOWARCOM: Hegseth's new U.S. Autonomous Warfare Command has a year to stand up, but its startup money is supposed to come from a reconciliation bill whose passage Defense One (October 25) describes as in doubt. John G. Ferrari, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and retired two-star general, told Defense One the Pentagon 'has little of the relevant force structure that earlier functional COCOMs could draw on': 'They have no idea... There's nobody on that stage that actually knows how to build anything like this.' The office is led by Owen West, who spoke at AUSA 2026 in October.

Ground robotics: Defense One reported (October 29) that two startups, working together for under a week, demonstrated a GPS-free inertial navigation package for small wheeled robots — the practical bottleneck for deploying ground-robot swarms. The test platform was Swarmbotics AI's FireAnt unmanned ground vehicles, exercised at a Joint Readiness Training Center rotation at Fort Polk on April 20, 2026.

Loitering munitions: Shephard's October drone digest notes that France activated an optional tranche of its February 2026 deal with KNDS France and Delair, triggering several hundred additional MX-10 Damocles rotary-wing loitering munitions on top of the original 460 units. Lithuania also advanced a loitering munition procurement. Shephard's Defence Insight forecasts global annual loitering munition spending rising nearly 50-fold between 2020 and 2029.

The counter-current: Shephard's October crewed-air review flags Israel's Apache deal as a bet on crewed aviation in an uncrewed age, and the U.S. Navy is keeping a Super Hornet production restart option open without a defined cost or timetable.
sections.whyItMatters: Unmanned warfare is being funded through unusual vehicles and built by companies with no institutional memory. The binding constraints right now are appropriations and navigation, not airframes.

sections.heading: Budgets: XM30 hollowed out, Golden Dome funded off-budget, and a watchdog dispute over interceptor stocks
sections.body:
U.S. FY2027 appropriations are already diverging sharply from the request.

XM30: The Army's first procurement buy of 19 XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicles at $546.99 million was cut by the House Appropriations Committee to $33.067 million, per H.Rept. 119-715, with the single note 'Program decrease—early to need.' The surviving figure matches, to the thousand dollars, the government-furnished equipment line in the Army's own P-5 cost analysis. The $290.069 million development line passed untouched. The Army plans 326 vehicles and $6.93 billion through FY2031, with the first production contract award scheduled for September 2027.

Golden Dome: The FY2027 request places roughly 98% of the program's $17.5 billion in mandatory funding, outside the ordinary appropriations process. Two Congressional Research Service products published a day apart disagree on the arithmetic: CRS R49023 (July 7) lists $17.5bn mandatory plus $0.40bn discretionary, summing to $17.9bn; CRS IF13264 (July 8) describes $17.5bn total with $17.1bn mandatory. The continuing resolution funding the government through December 11 does not mention Golden Dome at all.

Interceptors: CNN reported August 4, citing anonymous sources, that the U.S. had used 'nearly 80%' of its THAAD interceptors and roughly half its Patriot stock in the Iran war's opening campaign. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth rejected the claim on X the same day. CSIS put remaining THAAD interceptor stocks at about 250 as of July 2026, and a July 27 CSIS chart is titled 'Renewed Iran War Would Test Diminished Interceptor Inventories.' The figures remain contested and the underlying inventories are classified — treat the percentages as unverified.
sections.whyItMatters: Congress is buying equipment and skipping platforms. For XM30 the cut leaves the government-furnished gear with no vehicles to put it in, and Golden Dome's off-budget structure means a continuing resolution leaves it unprotected.

bottomLine: The day's developments share one theme: announced programmes and funded programmes are drifting apart. Ukraine's drone export reform has produced no permits, NATO's SYNC strategy explicitly disclaims legal and funding force while the GlobalEye deal it was headlined beside still has no signed contract, and the U.S. House cut the XM30's first buy by 94% on an 'early to need' finding. The exceptions run where localization is written into the contract — Saudi Arabia's Sarawat and Tuwaiq projects, Poland's $13bn naval pipeline — and where demand is undeniable, as with loitering munitions, forecast by Shephard to grow nearly 50-fold in the decade to 2029. Russia's cancellation of the Pyotr Velikiy is the mirror image: a $5 billion refit of its sister ship consumed the budget for a second. Procurement capacity, not procurement ambition, is the constraint heading into 2027.
sources: Defense-Aerospace, Naval News, TASS (via Naval News), Shephard Media / Defence Insight, Defense One, Breaking Defense (via Defense-Aerospace), Congressional Research Service (R49023, IF13264), CSIS, LB.ua (via Defense-Aerospace), Interfax-Ukraine (via Defense-Aerospace), AIN.ua (via Defense-Aerospace), Ohio Tax Credit Authority, H.Rept. 119-715, Saudi Ministry of Defense
